newsitem.title: GERMANY: ProSieben shares jump 32 pct on first trading day.
newsitem.headline: ProSieben shares jump 32 pct on first trading day.

text.p: Shares in German television network ProSieben AG jumped 32 percent as they traded for the first time on Monday, outstripping even major DAX companies with a traded volume of 2.7 million shares.
The preference shares, issued at a price of 72 marks ($41.2) in a flotation which was 50 times oversubscribed, ended at 95 marks.
Yet the closing price, just below an intraday high of 98 marks, was lower than many traders had hoped. In grey market trade early on Monday the stock had been changing hands at 106 to 110 marks.
The company promised to reward its new shareholders with dividend returns.
"We will pay a dividend and our dividend policy will be such that we can make our shareholders happy," ProSieben management board chairman Georg Kofler told Reuters Financial Television.
ProSieben board member Michael Woelfle told a news conference in Frankfurt he expected the company's television channels to keep expanding in the German advertising market.
The ProSieben group already makes more than 90 percent of its income with ad-financed television.

Woelfle said the group's largest station, ProSieben itself, had long-term growth potential of 20 percent from advertising and the company's number-two station, Kabel 1 would likely develop its advertising base at an even greater rate.

"Advertising customers are very interested in the connection between advertising-financed television and new media such as online services, " Woelfe said following ProSieben AG's first float on Monday morning.

"Therein lies significant potential for ProSieben AG as well," said Woelfle, who is also the chief executive of MediaGruppe Muenchen, a marketing and market research firm which counts ProSieben AG among its clients.

Kofler said the 360 million marks in initial stock proceeds would go towards TV programming. He distanced himself anew from plans to invest in pay TV, saying the costs and risks of applying for the right to participate were too great.

"At the moment ProSieben has the rights to free TV but not pay TV," Kofler told the news conference. "I think we spoke about it too early, but after looking into it, we made our decision (not to invest in pay television)."
ProSieben AG in September of last year shelved plans to roll out a pay TV channel called Sieben Plus.

ProSieben is the first German television broadcaster to list its shares on the stock market. The network said only one in 10 bidders had received any shares at all, and even winners had only gained a portion of the shares they ordered.
The issue price was at the top of the range announced last week at the end of the 10-day book-building period.
The listing raised 1.26 billion marks for the firm, increasing its capital by 360 million marks to over 700 million marks.
The issue is being managed by a banking consortium led by BHF-Bank AG, Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG, and Salomon Brothers.

A total 850 million shares were ordered although only 17.5 million will go on the market. The network said 52.5 percent of the issue will be placed with German individual investors. Thirty-three percent of the orders came from outside Germany.
Due to the high degree of oversubscription, the company said it used a complex lottery to fill the orders.
A German shareholder lobby group, Schutzgemeinschaft der Kleinaktionaere, said in answer to Reuter enquiries that it was satisfied with the way the lottery had been conducted.

ProSieben is also altering its shareholder structure to make Thomas Kirch, son of Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch, its majority shareholder with 60 percent of the ordinary voting shares. Retail group Rewe holds the remaining 40 percent.
($ = 1.747 German Marks)
